theme: God’s righteous judgment; circumcision of the heart
readingInstruction: Read Romans 2:1-29. Paul turns from the obvious sinners to the religious and moral person. Notice the standard of God’s judgment, and what Paul means by a Jew “inwardly.”
settingTheScene: After the dark picture in chapter 1, a Jewish reader might say, “Yes, those pagans deserve it!” Paul now closes the trap. In the style of a diatribe, a lively argument with an imaginary opponent, he shows that the moral person and the religious person are also under judgment. Having the Law, being circumcised, and belonging to the covenant people are not a shelter from God’s verdict. Paul’s point is that every mouth must be stopped (3:19).
observation: “Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things” (2:1).
“Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?” (2:4).
“He will render to each one according to his works” (2:6).
“For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified” (2:13).
“They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness” (2:15).
“On that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus” (2:16).
“But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (2:29).
interpretation:
Paul begins with the person who judges others: “You have no excuse.” Those who condemn others for the same sins they commit prove that they know right from wrong and fail to keep it. God’s judgment is according to truth. Then comes a lovely question: “Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?” God’s patience is not approval. It is a window of mercy. To ignore it is to store up wrath for the day of wrath.

God will “render to each one according to his works.” This sentence raises a question that students of Romans have asked for centuries: does Paul teach salvation by works? No. He is describing the standard of the final judgment. God will judge impartially, by works, because works reveal the heart. Eternal life goes to those who by patience in doing good seek glory and honor and immortality; wrath to those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth. But Paul will go on to show that no one meets this standard (3:9-20), and the believer’s works are the fruit and evidence of faith, not its foundation. The judgment according to works does not contradict justification by faith. It shows that real faith produces a changed life.

Paul next addresses the Jew who relies on the Law and boasts in God. He asks four hard questions: you teach others, do you teach yourself? You say not to steal, do you steal? Do you commit adultery? Do you rob temples? “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you,” he writes, quoting Isaiah 52:5. Circumcision has value if you keep the law, but if you break it, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. And an uncircumcised man who keeps the law’s requirements will be counted as circumcised.

The chapter closes with the center of the new covenant: “A Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter.” This echoes Deuteronomy 30:6 and Jeremiah 31:33. The true people of God are those whose hearts the Spirit has changed. Outward signs without inward reality count for nothing. This is a key text for progressive covenantalism: the promises made to Israel find their fulfillment in a people marked by the Spirit, Jew and Gentile together in Christ.
connection: Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6 call for circumcision of the heart. Jeremiah 9:25-26 and 31:31-34 speak of the heart and the new covenant. Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises the Spirit. Matthew 7:1-5 is Jesus on judging. Matthew 23 condemns hypocrisy. Ecclesiastes 12:14 says God will bring every deed into judgment. 2 Corinthians 5:10 says we must appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Philippians 3:3 says we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God. Galatians 6:15 says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but a new creation.
application:
Ask where you judge others for what you do yourself. Confess it.

Think of a time when God’s kindness led you to repentance. Thank him for it.

Examine whether your faith is outward or has reached the heart.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you judge others and excuse yourself.
Ask him to circumcise your heart.
Thank him for his kindness that leads you to repentance.
